title: Stopping the Snowball
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. describes a late-year intervention with his ninth-grade AP World History students: he invited those least likely to pass the exam to work in his room several times a week, using a list of study objectives he had prepared months earlier. The payoff was large for almost no extra effort, which left him wondering why he had waited until spring. He names the pattern Snowball Kids, students whose early-term problems become end-of-term emergencies regardless of the course level. His proposed fix is to move the same invitation to early in the school year, set by a phone reminder. The piece is a short, honest account of a simple, low-cost practice and an explicit hypothesis he intends to test.
points: Struggling students are often visible in the gradebook long before the crisis, so an early, direct invitation is cheap prevention.
The intervention required little teacher effort because the students worked from a pre-made list of study objectives.
The label Snowball Kids captures a pattern that cuts across advanced, standard and at-risk classes, especially when courses are demanding.
He treats the plan as a testable hypothesis, noting that an earlier meeting lacks a looming deadline and may draw fewer students.
quotes: After spring break of last year, I asked a handful of students, those who seemed to me least likely to earn college credit on the May 12 test, to come see me for lunch. In a very straightforward fashion, I explained why they were there and what I was asking them to do: come work in my classroom at least three times per week during the morning, lunch, and after-school slots that I had available.

Yet as May 12 got closer, I kept kicking myself: Why hadn’t I done this sooner? It was nearly zero effort on my part — the students just came in and worked from a list of study objectives I had created months ago — and it was reaping some big returns for the students. Couldn’t we have avoided a lot of stress and last-minute finagling?

It doesn’t matter if it’s an advanced class (a novel experience for me last year) or a standard class or an “at-risk” class, the phenomenon of Snowball Kids — kids for whose start-of-term problems snowball into end-of-term emergencies — seems to defy labeling, especially if our courses are as challenging as we want them to be.

Simple solutions are always better than complex solutions if both solutions achieve the same ends. I’m simply going to try bumping that post-spring-break meeting I held with kids to the early part of the school year, and then I want to see how it goes.

My hypothesis is that at least a couple of kids who might have Snowballed into the April Study Hall group will pull out of their descent and decrease their overall stress load for the year. If that happens for even one kid, I’ll consider it a professional gain. It doesn’t require me to work much harder, and it could potentially bring great benefit to my students.
